newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin renews NATO diplomacy, calls Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin renews NATO diplomacy, calls Chirac.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin began a round of telephone talks with Western leaders on Monday as Russia tries to work out final details of a new treaty with NATO within the next two weeks, the Kremlin said.
He made the first call to French President Jacques Chirac, who hopes to host the treaty signing in Paris on May 27.
"It was emphasised that solutions to the remaining difficult problems should be found, taking into account mutual security interests," the Kremlin said of Yeltsin's call to Chirac.

Yeltsin also plans to call a number of other NATO leaders in the coming days, a spokesman said. NATO Secretary General Javier Solana flies to Moscow on Tuesday for new negotiations with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

The Moscow-NATO deal is aimed at overcoming Russia's strong objections to the alliance's plans to expand eastwards to take in new members from the former Soviet bloc. Invitations to new members are due to go out at a NATO summit in Madrid in July.
Kremlin sources say Russia has already decided to sign a deal, but intends to keep up the uncertainty and anti-NATO rhetoric until the last minute to appease domestic opponents.
One Western diplomat in Moscow also said a deal looked likely.
"It looks as though we might get an agreement," the diplomat said. "It does not seem likely it will fall through, but there might be irritations and open questions until the very end."
The official said a previous disagreement over Moscow's insistence that NATO guarantee not to station nuclear weapons in new members' territory had been resolved.

Unsolved problems include differences over how the 1990 treaty governing conventional forces in Europe should be amended and whether a deal should contain a written NATO pledge not to deploy its military might in new member states.
The title of the agreement has also not been agreed upon, the Western diplomat said.
"There are still some loose ends, some issues which have to be resolved, and the negotiations will continue right until the end," Primakov said in a television interview aired on Sunday.
"But already on May 13 or 14, when Secretary-General Solana is in Moscow, it will be clear whether we can get to sign the document on May 27 or not."
Solana, who last met Primakov in Luxembourg last week, is due to arrive in Moscow on Tuesday afternoon and does not plan to meet reporters.
In an interview published in the Russian daily Izvestia on Monday, Primakov also sought to keep up the suspense.
"I want to reiterate that we are not pressed for time. We cannot sign a loose, ill-prepared document or one which does not suit us just because the French suggested the date of May 27," he said.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are thought be the leading contenders to join NATO, but Romania and Slovenia also hope to receive invitations from the alliance at the Madrid summit.
